## Deconstruct

### Original

The original data visualisation is the figure comparing margins of victory between male and female finalists in Joyner et al. (2025), *Evidence on sex differences in sports performance*, Journal of Applied Physiology. It is not reproduced here for copyright reasons; it can be viewed in the article at https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00615.2024.

It shows, for the top eight finishers in the men's and women's 800m and 10,000m runs and 100m and 1500m freestyle swims at a single Olympic Games, how far behind the winner each athlete finished, as a percentage of the winning time.


### Objective and Audience

The objective and audience of the original data visualisation chosen can be summarised as follows: 

#### Objective ####

**Question:**
The selected visualisation is aiming to portray and compare the different amount of variance in margin of victory between male and female athletes in Olympic running and swimming finals. The events chosen are the 10,000m and 800m run, and the 100m and 1500m freestyle swim.

**Answer:**
The visualisation shows that female athletes typically have a wider spread of finish times, compared to men, who appear to be relatively more "bunched up", particularly in the track events. Interestingly, the swim events appear to have similar dispersion of finish times when comparing genders. Additionally, the visualisation highlights the extremely narrow margins of victory at the elite level, most notably in the mens 10,000m

**So what?:**
Why do mens events seem to have tighter/closer finishes compare to womens events that are more spread out? 

#### Audience ####
This visualisation is presented in a peer reviewed journal article published by The Journal of Applied Physiology both online and in print. The intended audience of this paper and the visualisation are mainly physiologists and exercise scientists. Additionally, the authors of the paper specifically state that the paper highlights evidence for a framework to consider for policy decisions related to fairness in sport. Therefore members of governing bodies/policy makers and ethics experts may be interested in this paper. On top of that, educators and students in the sports science domain would likely make up another significant cohort of readers. There may also be potential interest from Medical experts, endocrinologists and reproductive experts. Lastly, as sex and gender has recently become somewhat topical, therefore journalists may be interested in reporting on the latest research related to gender differences in sports.

### Improvements

The original data visualisation chosen could be improved in the three following ways:

* **First improvement: **
The first issue with this visualisation is the repeating values/events on the y-axis. For example, "10,000m Run" is portrayed as the first event and again as the fifth event. The first appearance representing women (in red) and the second representing men (in blue). This makes comparison between males and females in the same event cumbersome and unintuitive. On top of this, the male and female colour encoding is buried in text (in the description) with no legend, adding an additional layer of difficulty to decipher this visualisation. To address this issue, an event will only appear on the y-axis once, and male and female data for that event will be aligned side-by-side with the existing colour encoding (with a legend) for easier comparison.

* **Second improvement: **
The visualisation only portrays four events at one Olympics. Drawing conclusions about differences between male and female performance in the selected events based on a single Olympic Games is not sufficient for fair or reliable inference. For example, how does the reader know (from the original visualisation) if the mens 10,000m race was an unusually close race, with all participants finishing within a narrow time frame? How do we know if the results seen in the original visualisation are applicable for all Olympic Games? The answer is, we don't know because the cohort is under-powered and may not be representative or transferable to other events. Therefore, by using additional data from the Olympics/World Aquatics websites, I will use faceting to include the finals of 3 other recent Olympics for the events given for the original visualisation. This will provide a more accurate depiction of patterns in the margins of victory in men vs women. 

* **Third improvement: **
It is relatively common at Olympic events for records to be broken. If a record is broken, this is potentially pertinent information to understand the spread of the top 8 athletes for a particular event. For example, if the mens 10000m race winner also broke a record, and this was noted on the visualisation, this would demonstrate that the entire field performed at an exceptional level. The original visualisation shows a significant gap between the gold medal winners and the rest of the pack in the womens 800m run and 100m freestyle. However, it is not communicated whether or not these races were won with record setting times with blistering performances, leaving the rest of the competition behind. This is vital contextual information that may completely alter a readers interpretation of the visualisation. To fix this problem, I will include records in the visualisation, highlighting the performances that were classed as either Olympic or world records.

## Reconstruct
### Code

The following code was used to improve the original. 

Data has been obtained through the official Olympic website (International Olympic Committee 2024). Some results for swimming were not available on the Olympics Games website, therefore some swimming results were obtained through the World Aquatics website (Formerly known as FINA) which is the world governing body for aquatic sports (World Aquatics, 2024). Data was manually input as there were no downloadable source files. This was an iterative process going in chronological order, extracting relevant track and swim events from the four most recent Olympics. 

#### Data Loading for London 2012 track events
(International Olympic Committee, 2012)
```{r}
library(tibble)
```

### Combining Data and Additional Feature Engineering

As the original data does not contain the percentage margin between athletes, this primary feature included in the original visualisation needed to be engineered. Additionally, for visualisation purposes, other features required some adjustment and engineering for presentation purposes.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Compile all results into one main data frame
olympic_results <- bind_rows(
  london2012track,
  london2012swim,
  rio2016track,
  rio2016swim,
  tokyo2020track,
  tokyo2020swim,
  paris2024track,
  paris2024swim
)

# Check frame
head(olympic_results)
# Look at data types
glimpse(olympic_results)

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(olympic_results)) # There are NA values in the records column as expected

# Change data types accordingly
olympic_results <- olympic_results %>%
  mutate(
    City = as.factor(City),
    Year = as.factor(Year),
    Event = as.factor(Event),
    Gender = as.factor(Gender),
    Country = as.factor(Country),
    Record = as.factor(Record)
  )

# Create function to convert time to seconds (Time has been entered as strings)
convert_time_to_seconds <- function(time_string) {
  if (is.na(time_string)) { # Create case for if time is null value
    return(NA)
  }
  if (grepl(":", time_string)) {# Case for events lasting >1min
    parts <- strsplit(time_string, ":")[[1]] # Split the string by colon
    minutes <- as.numeric(parts[1]) # First part of string is the minutes (convert to numeric)
    seconds <- as.numeric(parts[2]) # Second part of string is seconds (convert to numeric)
    total_seconds <- minutes * 60 + seconds # multiply minutes by 60 to get seconds and add seconds
  } else { # Case for when time < 1min
    total_seconds <- as.numeric(time_string) # Convert to numeric
  }
  return(total_seconds) # Return total_seconds
}

# Create new column of time in seconds for to calculate percent behind
olympic_results <- olympic_results %>%
  mutate(Time_seconds = sapply(Time, convert_time_to_seconds)) %>% # Apply newly created function
  group_by(City, Year, Event, Gender) %>% # In order to extract the winner for each event, we need to ensure we are selecting times for only one event
  mutate(
    Winner_time = min(Time_seconds, na.rm = TRUE), # Create a new column of winner times (min = fastest time)
    Percent_behind = 100 * (Time_seconds - Winner_time) / Winner_time # Create a new column of % behind which will be used for visualisation
  ) %>%
  ungroup() # ungroup

olympic_results <- olympic_results %>% # Join Olympics and Year for labelling in visualisation
  mutate(
      Olympics_Label = paste(City, Year, sep = "\n"),
      Olympics_Label = factor(Olympics_Label, 
        levels = c(  # Add factorisation to ensure order is applied when visualising
          "London\n2012",
          "Rio\n2016",
          "Tokyo\n2020",
          "Paris\n2024")))

olympic_results <- olympic_results %>% 
  mutate(Event = factor(Event, levels = c(  # Add factorisation to ensure order is applied when visualising
    "800m",
    "10000m",
    "100m Freestyle",
    "1500m Freestyle"
  )))

olympic_results <- olympic_results %>% # Add a new variable 'sport' this is done to add a background colour later according to sport making the visualisation more intuitive to read
  mutate(
    Sport = case_when(
      Event %in% c("800m", "10000m") ~ "Track",
      Event %in% c("100m Freestyle", "1500m Freestyle") ~ "Swimming"
    )
  )

olympic_results <- olympic_results %>% # Convert to factor for visualisation
  mutate(
    Sport = as.factor(Sport))

# Same for records
olympic_results$RecordType <- factor(olympic_results$Record, levels = c("WR", "OR"))

olympic_results$RecordType <- case_when( # Create new variable for labelling/legend in visualisation
  olympic_results$Record == "WR" ~ "World Record",
  olympic_results$Record == "OR" ~ "Olympic Record",
  TRUE ~ NA_character_ # all other cases 
)

olympic_results$Event <- recode( # Adjust labelling for better design in plot
  olympic_results$Event,
  "100m Freestyle" = "100m\nFreestyle",
  "1500m Freestyle" = "1500m\nFreestyle"
)

olympic_results$Event <- recode( # Adjust labelling for better design in plot
  olympic_results$Event,
  "10000m" = "10000m\nRun",
  "800m" = "800m\nRun"
)

panel_bg <- olympic_results %>% # Create a new data frame for facet/panel colour coding by sport
  distinct(Event, Olympics_Label, Sport) %>% # Ensure every event is included
  mutate(
    xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, # Mandatory fields for geom_rect
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, # Mandatory fields for geom_rect
    bg_fill = ifelse(Sport == "Track", "#fbeee6", "#ebf5fb")  # Assign colour codes
  )

```
### Plot Generation
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggnewscale)

# Plot
p1 <- ggplot(olympic_results, aes(x = Percent_behind, y = Gender)) + 
  facet_grid(Event ~ Olympics_Label, switch = "y") +

  #Background rectangles (facet colouring based on sport)
  geom_rect(data = panel_bg,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = bg_fill),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = NA,
    alpha = 1
  ) +
  
  # Ensures fill for geom_rect is kept as 'bg_fill' values and removes unnecessary legend
  scale_fill_identity(guide = "none") + 
  
  # Adds "grid-lines". "Normal" method of adding gridlines was overlapped by geom_rect objects
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = seq(0, max(olympic_results$Percent_behind, na.rm = TRUE), by = 1),
    color = "gray85",
    size = 0.3
  ) +
  
  # Used to be able to use scale_fill for multiple geoms
  new_scale_fill() +
  # Main gender-based points
  geom_point(
    aes(shape = Gender, fill = Gender),
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.65,
    stroke = NA,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)
  ) +

  # Diamonds for records
  geom_point(
    data = subset(olympic_results, !is.na(RecordType)), # Exclude all results without a record
    aes(color = RecordType, shape = Gender),
    shape = 23, # Diamond shape
    alpha = 1,
    size = 3.5,
    stroke = 1.5,
    fill = NA,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +

  # Manual aesthetics
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Men" = 21, "Women" = 24)) +
  
  # Add manual colours for gender geoms
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Gender", values = c("Men" = "#1f77b4", "Women" = "#d62728")) +
  
  # Add manual colours for record geoms
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Record",
    values = c("Olympic Record" = "#FF8C00", "World Record" = "#FFD700")
  ) +

  # Add labels
  labs(
    x = "Percent (Time) Behind 1st Place",
    y = "",
    title = "Margins of Victory in Olympic Finals:\nTop 8 Finishers by Gender",
    caption = "*Womens 1500m freestyle
                was not an event
              in 2012 or 2016"
  ) +
  
  # Add vertical line representing finish line - allows for more intuitive understanding of visualisation
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  
  # Add minimal theme
  theme_minimal() +
  
  # Add manual theme elements
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"), # adjust position and appearance of title
    strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"), # Make Olympic Games 'bold'
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(), # Remove gender text
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"), # Increase panel spacing to improve readability
    legend.position = "right", # Position legend
    plot.caption =  element_text(hjust = 1.41, vjust = 2, face = "italic", size = 8), # Adjust position and appearance of caption
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12, margin = margin(t = 15)) # Adjust position and appearance of x-axis label
  ) +
  
  # Stops geom objects near edge of facet plots being "clipped off"
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  
  # Adjusts settings for legend
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(order = 1, title = "Gender", override.aes = list(stroke = 0)), # Stops outline appearing on legend
    shape = guide_legend(order = 1), # Stops legend appearing with additional gender information
    color = guide_legend(order = 2, title = "Record", override.aes = list(shape = 23, fill = NA, stroke = 1.5, size = 3)) # adjusts Legend for records
  )

```
### Reconstruction

The following plot improves the original data visualisation in the three ways previously explained.

```{r fig.align="center", echo = FALSE, out.width="100%"}
p1
```
